title: ORM & data access
summary: What an ORM buys you and what it costs, the N+1 query trap, transactions and the repository pattern, and when to drop to raw SQL — shown with JPA/Hibernate.
note:
1. ORM maps rows↔objects so you write Java, not SQL strings
2. Benefits: less boilerplate, type safety, portability; cost: hidden queries
3. N+1: one query for the list, then one per row — fix with a join/fetch
4. Wrap related writes in a transaction; use a repository to isolate data access
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
recall.a: Loading a list runs 1 query, then lazily loading a relation per row runs N more — N+1 round trips. Fix with a join fetch or batch fetch.

recall.q: Why wrap multi-step writes in a transaction?
recall.a: So the group commits all-or-nothing; a failure midway rolls back, keeping data consistent (atomicity).

recall.q: When drop the ORM for raw SQL?
recall.a: Heavy reporting, bulk updates, or finely tuned queries where the generated SQL is slow or awkward.

shot.title: ORM vs raw SQL
shot.body:
| | ORM (JPA) | Raw SQL / JDBC |
|---|---|---|
| boilerplate | low | high |
| control over SQL | indirect | full |
| portability | high | DB-specific |
| N+1 risk | easy to hit | explicit |
| best for | CRUD domains | tuned reads, bulk ops |

sections.title: What an ORM does
sections.body: ✍️ An **Object-Relational Mapper** maps database rows to objects and back, so you query with method calls and objects instead of hand-written SQL. In Java the standard is **JPA**, implemented by **Hibernate**. You get less boilerplate, compile-time type safety, and DB portability — at the cost of SQL being generated out of sight.

sections.title: The N+1 trap
sections.body:
✍️ The classic ORM pitfall: fetch a list of orders (1 query), then touch each order's customer, triggering a **lazy** query per row — N more. 100 orders = 101 queries.
- Fix with an eager **join fetch** (`JOIN FETCH o.customer`), an `@EntityGraph`, or batch fetching. Always inspect the SQL the ORM actually emits.
